catalog_quote: Gussenhoven 2000 (Roermond): "Within the word, two types of restriction conspire to confine the tonal contrast to certain locations. Firstly, the contrast is restricted to the syllable with main stress. The dialect of Roermond has the same stress system as standard Dutch. Main stress falls on either of the rightmost two syllables of the word if the penult is closed, and on one of the last three rightmost syllables if the penult is open. A final syllable without main word stress can be strong, i.e. form a foot. Secondly, the contrast is restricted to syllables with two sonorant moras. Thus, the syllable rime must contain a long vowel, a diphthong, or a lax vowel followed by a sonorant consonant ... in order for the contrast to exist. As a result, words whose main-stressed syllable contains only a single sonorant mora have neither Accent I nor Accent II." Peters 2006 (Hasselt): "Stress lo…

audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are verbatim in the held files at the stated locators (Gussenhoven 2000 ROA-382 sec. 2.0 p. 2; Peters 2006 ms sections 'Stress' and 'Tone'). (2) The classification (Dutch-type quantity-sensitive right-edge window, 'weight-hedged') rests on an explicit rule statement by the leading authority on Limburgian prosody in a phonology article, corroborated by a JIPA Illustration for the second variety; the newly fetched sources Gussenhoven & Peters 2008 survey (DBNL, p. 90, p. 105) is consistent (tone locus = word-stressed syllable; sentence accent as in Standard Dutch; antepenult-stressed words with final secondary stress) but silent on the placement algorithm. (3) Glottolog's descriptive list for limb1263 is 1877-1939 dialect monographs plus a tone-perception dissertation; the held Houben 1905 has no stress-rule section.
